issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

issues.explanation: The trigger 'my ex' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma and with the rest of the profile, which centers on danger/vigilance cues (blood, temperature, hypervigilance, sleep vigilance, inability to feel safe). This relationship-specific reminder suggests a different interpersonal trauma context that is not represented elsewhere in Threat or other nodes, making the trigger set clinically incoherent for the same index trauma.

vignette:
Omar, a 29-year-old train conductor, presented to the clinic with a pervasive sense of unease and hyper-alertness that had steadily intensified since a horrific incident he witnessed nearly eight months prior. He was single, and his quiet, watchful demeanor hinted at the internal struggle he described. The trauma occurred late one winter night when, during his shift as a conductor, his train struck a person who had wandered onto the tracks. Though he wasn't driving, he was the first to reach the scene after the emergency stop, forced to confront the devastating aftermath. The image of the victim’s visible injuries, the unsettling stillness of the body, and the specific temperature of the cold, damp night air clinging to his skin as he waited for first responders, were seared into his memory. A small, dark smear of blood on the concrete near the tracks had also caught his eye, an image that still flashed through his mind without warning.

In the months that followed, Omar found his world shrinking, his senses perpetually on high alert. He described how a sudden chill on his skin, particularly when he was out in the evening or walking near the train yard, would instantly plunge him into a state of intense vigilance. The sensation would trigger a visceral internal alarm, making his heart pound and his breath catch, as if he were back at the scene of the accident. Similarly, encountering visual cues like blood, even a small cut on a coworker's finger, or seeing visible injuries on others, such as a passenger with a bandaged arm, immediately activated a profound sense of threat. In these moments, Omar’s entire system would become superalert and watchful, his eyes darting, constantly scanning his surroundings for any sign of impending danger. He found himself unable to relax, convinced that something terrible was about to happen again.

This constant state of hypervigilance had become a heavy burden, especially at work. Each time he was on the train, the familiar hum of the engine or the fleeting sight of something red outside the window could set off his internal alarm, making it impossible to focus. What frightened him most was the deep-seated certainty that he could not trust safety, even when his colleagues or supervisors assured him that all protocols were followed and the tracks were clear. Their words felt hollow, unable to penetrate the core belief that danger was always lurking just out of sight, ready to strike without warning. This profound inability to believe in his own safety extended beyond his work environment, seeping into every aspect of his life. At home, he struggled profoundly with sleep. He would lie awake for hours, his mind refusing to switch off, needing to stay alert to every creak of the floorboards or distant siren. His body, he felt, was constantly on guard, convinced it needed to protect him from an unseen threat, making restful sleep an elusive luxury.

The cumulative effect of this unrelenting threat response was debilitating. Omar had started declining social invitations, preferring to stay home where he felt he had more control over his environment, though even there, true peace eluded him. He had taken to meticulously checking all the locks on his apartment door multiple times before bed, a ritual that offered only fleeting reassurance. The exhaustion from chronic sleep deprivation, combined with the mental toll of constant vigilance, began to impact his performance at work, making it harder to concentrate on his duties. He knew he couldn't continue living this way, perpetually trapped in a state of fear and distrust. He finally sought help, hoping to find a way to reclaim his life from the shadow of that dreadful night, but deep down, he was terrified that the world truly was as unsafe as his mind insisted it was.
